newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-NORMAN PREFERS DESIGNING TO PLAYING.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-NORMAN PREFERS DESIGNING TO PLAYING.

text.p: World number one Greg Norman conceded on Wednesday that he is not fired up for golf right now and that his growing course design business is more fun.
"I get a lot more enjoyment out of the design work than jumping in a plane for a week to go and play golf somewhere," the Australian said.

On the eve of the Alfred Dunhill Cup team event on the Old Course at St Andrews -- a place which inspires golfers from around the world -- Norman, 41 and an international player for 20 years, admitted to feeling jaded.
"I do not think I will be charged up again until next year," he said. "By then I won't have played much in a while and I'll be ready to start firing again."
He plans only four more events this year and one early in January and already he has decided not to play more than 15 events on next year's U.S. Tour.
But he is not just going through the motions this week as he links with Steve Elkington and Wayne Riley in a bid to win this team title for the first time since 1986.
"Australia have not done the job we wanted the last couple of years and this time we are a little more keyed up and eager," he said.

Norman, who so memorably lost this year's Masters to Nick Faldo after a final-round 78, said he has 28 courses under contract in various stages of development, mostly in Asia but with some in Central America and some in the United States, where he lives.
"I just finished one called Sugarbush near Atlanta and the U.S. PGA are going to play the BellSouth Classic there next year.
"I'm surprised the PGA have come in so soon and I take an enormous amount of pride from it. They have paid great credit to my ability to design a course up to that standard," he said.
He said his business has expanded greatly over the past 18 months. "I would say it's just about comparable to my position as a player.
"I never thought five years ago I would be so involved in design or enjoying it so much."
But the winner of two British Opens among some 70 victories around the world said he is not close to hanging up his clubs just yet.
"I'm just enjoying doing two things now. I'll probably play 22 or 23 tournaments next year. I've been saying since 1993 that in the year 2000 I'll sit back and take stock.
"I have no intention of giving the game up yet. I want to focus on my golf for the next three to four years.
"My desire for championships has not diminished. I am still keen to play. I am still competitive.
"I might go on past 2000. But if I do stop then, it will be on a high note," he said.
